title: What is contract testing — testing the agreement (contract) between two services: the CONSUMER says "I expect this response shape" and the PROVIDER says "I will always return this shape" — and what tool is used (Pact)?
shortTitle: What is contract testing and the tool used

s1_definition.profdef: Contract testing verifies the agreement between two services about the shape and semantics of their interaction, independently of running both together. The consumer declares the requests it will send and the responses it expects, which forms a contract, and the provider is verified against that contract to confirm it will always return what the consumer needs. This catches integration breakages at the boundary without a full end-to-end environment. The standard tool is Pact, which supports consumer-driven contract testing where the consumer generates the contract and the provider verifies against it, typically coordinated through a Pact Broker.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the mobile-app team (the consumer) depends on the accounts service (the provider) to return a balance in a certain shape. Contract testing is like a written agreement between the two teams: the app team writes down exactly what it sends and what fields and types it expects back, and the accounts team is checked against that written agreement to guarantee it will always send that shape. The beauty is that neither team needs the whole bank running to test this; the app team tests against a recorded promise, and the accounts team is verified against the same promise. If the accounts team ever changes the response in a way that would break the app, the check fails before anything ships. Pact is the tool that records and enforces this agreement.
s1_definition.oneliner: Contract testing verifies the agreement between a consumer and a provider, the consumer states the request and expected response shape and the provider is verified to always return it, catching boundary breakages without full end-to-end, using a tool like Pact with a Pact Broker.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Contract testing verifies the agreement between two services about the shape and semantics of their interaction, independently of running both together. The consumer declares the requests it will send and the responses it expects, which forms a contract, and the provider is verified against that contract to confirm it will always return what the consumer needs. This catches integration breakages at the boundary without a full end-to-end environment. The standard tool is Pact, which supports consumer-driven contract testing where the consumer generates the contract and the provider verifies against it, typically coordinated through a Pact Broker.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the mobile-app team (the consumer) depends on the accounts service (the provider) to return a balance in a certain shape. Contract testing is like a written agreement between the two teams: the app team writes down exactly what it sends and what fields and types it expects back, and the accounts team is checked against that written agreement to guarantee it will always send that shape. The beauty is that neither team needs the whole bank running to test this; the app team tests against a recorded promise, and the accounts team is verified against the same promise. If the accounts team ever changes the response in a way that would break the app, the check fails before anything ships. Pact is the tool that records and enforces this agreement.

**One line to remember:** Contract testing verifies the agreement between a consumer and a provider, the consumer states the request and expected response shape and the provider is verified to always return it, catching boundary breakages without full end-to-end, using a tool like Pact with a Pact Broker.

sections.s2_technical:
Contract testing sits between unit tests and full end-to-end tests and targets a specific risk: that two independently deployed services drift apart at their interface. In a consumer-driven approach, the consumer writes tests against a mock of the provider, specifying the requests it makes and the responses it expects, down to the fields, types, and relevant values. Running those consumer tests produces a contract, a machine-readable document describing the interactions the consumer relies on. The provider then runs verification: it replays each interaction from the contract against the real provider and checks that the actual response satisfies what the consumer expected. If the provider's response no longer matches, the verification fails, flagging a breaking change before deployment.

The key property is that the two sides are tested independently, without standing up both services together. The consumer test uses a local mock driven by the contract, so it is fast and isolated, and the provider verification runs against the provider alone. This avoids the cost, flakiness, and slowness of a full integration environment while still catching the integration risk that unit tests miss, namely that the provider returns what the consumer actually needs. Contract tests focus on the shape and semantics of the interaction, the structure, required fields, and types, rather than exhaustive business logic, which stays in each service's own tests.

Pact is the de facto tool for consumer-driven contract testing. The consumer uses Pact to define expected interactions and generate a pact file, the contract. That pact is shared with the provider, commonly via a Pact Broker, which stores contracts, versions them, and tracks which consumer and provider versions are compatible. The provider uses Pact to verify itself against the pact, and the Broker's can-I-deploy capability lets a pipeline check whether a given provider or consumer version is safe to deploy against the versions currently in each environment, which is how contract testing becomes a deployment gate. This flips the usual direction: instead of the provider defining an API and hoping consumers cope, the consumers express their real needs and the provider guarantees them.

The senior nuances are that contract testing verifies the interface agreement, not full behavior, so it complements rather than replaces unit tests and a thin layer of end-to-end tests. It is consumer-driven, so it captures exactly what consumers rely on, which both prevents the provider from breaking them and frees the provider to change anything no consumer depends on. The Pact Broker and can-I-deploy are what make it operationally valuable, turning contracts into automated compatibility gates in CI/CD. You should keep contracts focused on structure and essential semantics, use flexible matchers for values that vary rather than pinning exact data, and treat a contract change as a coordination event between teams. There is also provider-driven or schema-based contract testing, for example using OpenAPI, which suits public APIs with many unknown consumers, whereas consumer-driven Pact suits internal microservices with known consumers. In a bank with many services, contract testing is what lets teams deploy independently and frequently without fear that a change to the accounts service silently breaks the mobile app, which is exactly the safety a fast-moving microservice organization needs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India mobile app consumes the accounts service's balance endpoint and relies on specific fields and types, so it must declare what it expects as a contract. This is exactly the consumer side.

Problem 2 — The accounts service must be verified to always return that shape, so a change that drops or renames a field is caught before deploy. This is exactly provider verification.

Problem 3 — Neither team should need the whole system running, and a Broker should gate deploys, which is exactly Pact plus can-I-deploy.

In the mini-project we model a consumer that declares an expected contract, a provider that produces a response, and a verifier that checks the provider's response against the contract, demonstrating a passing case and a breaking change caught, plus notes on Pact. We write a Java harness.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
qa-contract/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/java/com/bank/qa/contract/
│   │   ├── ContractDemo.java       (main runnable demo)
│   │   ├── Contract.java           (consumer's expected shape)
│   │   ├── AccountsProvider.java   (provider response — may change)
│   │   └── ContractVerifier.java   (verify provider vs contract)
│   └── test/java/com/bank/qa/contract/
│       └── ContractVerifierTest.java (Pact in a real project)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/qa/contract/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.qa.contract.ContractDemo

# Real Pact flow:
#   consumer test → generates pact file → publish to Pact Broker
#   provider test → verifies against pact from Broker
#   pipeline: pact-broker can-i-deploy --to-environment production
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a consumer contract declaring that the balance response must contain an account identifier as a string, a balance as a number, and a currency as a string, and two provider versions, one compatible and one with a breaking change.

Step 1: The consumer, the mobile app, declares its expected shape as the contract, capturing exactly the fields and types it relies on, which is the consumer-driven step.

Step 2: The verifier checks the compatible provider's response against the contract; every required field is present with the expected type, so it passes, meaning the provider is safe to deploy against this consumer.

Step 3: The verifier then checks the breaking provider version, which renamed balance to amount and changed it from a number to a string.

Step 4: The verifier detects that the required balance field is missing and reports a contract violation, failing the verification, which is exactly the breaking change being caught at the boundary before anything is deployed.

Step 5: The demo notes that in real tooling Pact does this properly, the consumer generates a pact file, the provider verifies against it, and a Pact Broker with can-I-deploy gates the pipeline so an incompatible provider or consumer version cannot be promoted.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 10:40:40 [INFO] === Provider verification: compatible version ===
2026-10-30 10:40:40 [INFO] Contract satisfied -> PASS (safe to deploy)
2026-10-30 10:40:40 [INFO] === Provider verification: BREAKING change (renamed/retyped) ===
2026-10-30 10:40:40 [SEVERE] CONTRACT VIOLATION: missing field 'balance'
2026-10-30 10:40:40 [INFO] Contract satisfied -> FAIL (blocked BEFORE deploy)
2026-10-30 10:40:40 [INFO] Real tooling: Pact — consumer generates pact file, provider verifies, Pact Broker + can-I-deploy gates the pipeline.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  CONSUMER (mobile app) test against provider MOCK
    │ declares requests + expected response shape
    ▼
  Pact file (the CONTRACT) → Pact Broker (stores + versions)
    │
    ▼
  PROVIDER (accounts svc) verification: replay interactions
    │ actual response satisfies contract?
    ├─ yes → PASS (safe)
    └─ no  → FAIL (breaking change caught BEFORE deploy)
    │
    ▼
  Broker can-i-deploy → pipeline gate (compatible versions only)
  (tested INDEPENDENTLY — no full end-to-end env needed)
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Contract Verification ═══

  ┌─ Flow ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ consumer: declare interactions → generate pact        │
  │ broker  : store + version contracts                   │
  │ provider: replay pact → assert response matches       │
  │ gate    : can-i-deploy(version, environment)          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  verifies SHAPE/semantics (fields, types), not full logic
  use flexible matchers for varying values

  ── Class Diagram ───────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────┐ checks ┌──────────────────┐
  │ ContractVerifier │───────▶│ Contract         │
  │ + verify(c,actual)│        │ expected: field→type
  └──────────────────┘        └──────────────────┘
          against ▲ AccountsProvider.getBalance()

  ── State Diagram: a provider change ────────────────────
  [compatible] → verify PASS → [deployable]
  [breaking]   → verify FAIL → [blocked]

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────
  1. consumer declares Contract
  2. verify(contract, compatible response) → PASS
  3. verify(contract, breaking response) → FAIL
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Contract testing verifies the agreement between two services about the shape and semantics of their interaction, independently of running both together. In the consumer-driven approach, the consumer writes tests against a mock of the provider, declaring the requests it sends and the responses it expects down to the fields and types, and running those tests produces a contract, a machine-readable document of exactly what the consumer relies on. The provider is then verified by replaying each interaction from the contract against the real provider and checking the actual response satisfies the expectation. If the provider's response no longer matches, verification fails, flagging a breaking change before deployment.

The key property is that the two sides are tested independently, without standing up both services together, so the consumer test uses a fast local mock and the provider verification runs against the provider alone. That avoids the cost and flakiness of a full integration environment while still catching the integration risk that unit tests miss, that the provider actually returns what the consumer needs. Contract tests focus on structure, required fields, and types, not exhaustive business logic, which stays in each service's own tests. The standard tool is Pact: the consumer uses it to generate a pact file, which is shared via a Pact Broker that stores and versions contracts and tracks compatibility, and the provider uses Pact to verify itself against the pact. The Broker's can-I-deploy check lets a pipeline confirm whether a given version is safe to deploy against the versions currently in each environment, which turns contracts into automated deployment gates.

The nuances I add are that contract testing complements rather than replaces unit tests and a thin end-to-end layer, that being consumer-driven captures exactly what consumers rely on, which both protects them and frees the provider to change anything no consumer depends on, and that the Broker and can-I-deploy are what make it operationally valuable. At the National Bank of India our mobile app consumed the accounts service, and before contract testing a backend change once renamed a response field and broke the app in production. With Pact, the consumer's contract declared it needed a numeric balance field, and when a provider change would have dropped or retyped it, the provider verification failed in CI and can-I-deploy blocked the release, so teams could deploy independently and frequently without silently breaking each other. Being able to explain the consumer-states-expectation, provider-is-verified flow, the independence from end-to-end, and Pact with the Broker and can-I-deploy is what shows an interviewer I understand contract testing as the safety that lets microservices evolve without fear.
